content:
Extreme heat warning auto-issued yellow

The Labour Department today announced a new mechanism that continues to use the Observatory's Heat Index, adding two new conditions on top of the existing warning trigger criteria to lower the activation thresholds. The first condition is that when the Observatory issues an Extreme Heat Weather Special Alert, the authorities will automatically issue a yellow Heat Stress at Work warning, while also lowering the thresholds for the red and black warnings. Previously, issuing a red warning required the Heat Index to reach 32 or above at King's Park monitoring station or at four out of the remaining nine monitoring stations. Under the new mechanism, if the Observatory has already issued an Extreme Heat Weather Special Alert, a reading of 32 at King's Park or at just two out of the remaining nine stations will suffice to trigger the red warning. According to Observatory data, the "Extreme Heat Weather" Special Alert is issued when the temperature has reached or is expected to generally reach an extreme level, i.e. 35.0 degrees or above, reminding the public that the weather is extremely hot and to pay attention to their physical health.

If multiple areas hit 35°C with enough data to trigger yellow, it will "upgrade" directly to red

Another new condition in the new mechanism is that when temperatures across multiple areas of Hong Kong reach 35 degrees or above, in addition to further lowering the index thresholds for triggering warnings, the existing Heat Stress at Work warnings will automatically be upgraded by one level. Hui Chak-sum gave an example: if multiple areas reach above 35 degrees with sufficient data to trigger a yellow warning, it will directly "upgrade" to a red warning; when the threshold for a red warning is reached, a black warning will be issued directly.

The new mechanism takes effect tomorrow (28th). Hui Chak-sum said although this year's summer holidays are nearly over, hot weather may persist, and it is impossible to estimate whether temperatures will rise abnormally again. The new mechanism can then be applied. Two former directors of the Observatory earlier wrote that the authorities had misused the Observatory's Heat Index, arguing that it failed to reflect the conditions endured by outdoor workers, and suggested adopting the Wet Bulb Globe Temperature used by many countries. The Labour Department said it would continue to review the mechanism's operation after its launch and keep improving it, such as studying whether to incorporate Wet Bulb Globe Temperature monitoring data as one of the system's indicators.

Under the new mechanism, the hottest day on 9 August would have triggered a red warning

After the Labour Department chief briefed the media, the department further explained to the press, giving an example that on 9 August, when temperatures broke records, a red Heat Stress at Work warning would have been issued under the new mechanism. On 8 August, temperatures were relatively lower, but wind speed and humidity were unfavourable, potentially triggering a black warning. Under the new mechanism, there may be four to seven days per year with a red warning issued, and one to two days per year potentially with a black warning.

Lam Chiu-ying: Continuing to use Hong Kong Heat Index is a "defect to be addressed"

Former Observatory director Lam Chiu-ying, who has repeatedly criticised the current Heat Stress at Work warning mechanism, described the new arrangement as "a step forward," believing that incorporating temperature into consideration is a down-to-earth and easily grasped indicator for workers, meeting the expectations of frontline workers. However, he described the continued use of the Hong Kong Heat Index in the warning mechanism as a "defect to be addressed," saying, "There is no reason for us to use an unscientific (mechanism) as the foundation and then use other methods to correct it." He hopes the authorities will formally adopt the internationally used Wet Bulb Globe Temperature before next summer. Lam Chiu-ying also pointed out that the thresholds for issuing warnings are only the starting point; the measures to cool down workers are merely guidelines, and workers have reported that they are rarely effectively implemented. He suggested making these measures statutory requirements.

Lee Boon-ying: New mechanism is a "minor patch"

Another former director, Lee Boon-ying, also reiterated that the Hong Kong Heat Index research is not applicable to outdoor workers, and the Labour Department's application of the Hong Kong Heat Index is "scientifically untenable." He described the new mechanism's main addition of considering temperature as a "minor patch" that fails to fully account for humidity, wind, and other factors, saying it "only addresses the predicament of having no higher-level Heat Stress at Work warning during extreme high temperatures," emphasising that Wet Bulb Globe Temperature has proven effective in many countries. He said Hong Kong's hot weather has not yet passed, and the protection for outdoor workers remains inadequate; they can only look out for themselves.

ICRC suggests subsidising Wet Bulb Globe Index equipment at worksites

The Industrial Casualties Rights Committee said it is pleased to see the authorities optimising the mechanism, noting that the Observatory's Extreme Heat Weather Special Alert has a预警 nature. Incorporating the special alert into consideration, it is believed, will make it easier to trigger higher-level warnings, reflecting the heat stress faced by outdoor workers. The committee also suggested that the government promote and subsidise companies in installing Wet Bulb Globe Index monitoring equipment at worksites, so that employers can adjust work arrangements according to on-site conditions.

The committee also pointed out that if workers' working conditions do not improve after warnings are issued, the warnings are as good as useless. It suggested improving the existing "Guidelines on Prevention of Heat Stroke at Work" to stipulate that when a black warning is issued, high-risk outdoor work must be suspended; for other levels, it suggested guaranteeing that workers can take rest as needed without punishment from employers.

Greenpeace said this adjustment is old wine in a new bottle. By not using Wet Bulb Globe Temperature and continuing to use the "Hong Kong Heat Index" that does not meet practical needs, it fails to reflect the actual heat stress faced by outdoor workers, offering limited protection. Greenpeace Project Officer Yeung Kit-lai said this update is like scratching an itch through a boot. She pointed out that the conditions for issuing red and black Heat Stress at Work warnings remain based on the Hong Kong Heat Index, which has a relatively low weighting for "heat radiation," making it unsuitable for measuring the heat stress of outdoor workers and lacking a scientific basis. She said the Labour Department's continued use of incorrect indicators significantly reduces protection for workers.
